findings.title: D69-SEC-001 regression: QR-confirmed baseUrl flows unvalidated from upstream into all iLink calls
findings.description: Re-checked post-D69: D69 T4 did not ship the baseUrl host allowlist (D69-SEC-001 fix_hint). interpretQrStatus still returns `baseUrl: String(response['baseurl'] ?? '')` as plain string at packages/adapters/src/wechat/ilink.ts:221, wechat-login.ts:78 writes it into .env verbatim via upsertWechatEnvFile, and joinUrl uses it as the base for every subsequent ilinkGet/ilinkPost (ilink.ts:98,165). A compromised or hostile iLink QR-status response can redirect ALL outbound iLink traffic (including credentialed token-bearing calls) to attacker-controlled host.
findings.evidence: cli/src/wechat-login.ts:78 `baseUrl: action.baseUrl || currentBase`; packages/adapters/src/wechat/ilink.ts:221 `baseUrl: String(response['baseurl'] ?? '')`; joinUrl() at ilink.ts:98,165; assertWechatCdnUrl (ilink-media.ts:98) exists for CDN only, NOT for QR-confirmed baseUrl
findings.fix_hint: Validate baseUrl against known iLink host set (ilinkai.weixin.qq.com, etc.) before persisting; reject unknown hosts in wechat-login.ts:78 with a clear error.

findings.title: D69-SEC-005 regression: Owner routes still lack per-IP/per-subject rate limiting
findings.description: D70 pre-scoped SEC-5. Re-checked: no rate-limit middleware on owner-routes. createOwnerRoutes wires 9 register*Routes (owner-routes.ts:18-27) — every handler only calls `ownerAuthorized(c)` and then proceeds. /v1/owner/documents:50 (list), /v1/owner/memories:35 (list 1-100/page), /v1/owner/audit/fatigue (batch caps 1000 ids) have NO rate limit at the Hono layer. The wechat-sweeper-notify.ts:62 throttle exists but is a sweeper-only helper. A compromised loopback caller or runaway local script can hammer expensive endpoints (audit-fatigue batch / mcp status / conversations-schedule).
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/owner-routes.ts:18-27 (no middleware between createOwnerRoutes and register*); owner-routes/*.ts all start with `if (!ownerAuthorized(c)) return c.text(...)` then immediately process; grep 'rate' / 'throttle' returns 0 hits in owner-routes/
findings.fix_hint: Add an app.use('/v1/owner/*', slidingWindowThrottle) middleware with a small per-IP window (e.g. 60 req/min) and a per-endpoint batch cap. Mirror the wechat-sweeper-notify.ts:62 in-memory throttle pattern.

findings.title: D69-SEC-008 regression: MCP HTTP/SSE transport still has no SSRF guard for private/loopback/link-local
findings.description: D70 pre-scoped SEC-8. Re-checked: parseMcpConnectionConfig only validates URL scheme (mcp-config.ts:175) — `if (parsed.protocol !== 'http:' && parsed.protocol !== 'https:')`. No hostname IP-range check. http-transport.ts:44 and sse-transport.ts:69 issue fetchFn(config.url) with the Bearer token from BUTLER_V5_MCP_TOKEN in the Authorization header. An operator who misconfigures BUTLER_V5_MCP_URL (or a malicious manifest entry) can target http://10.0.0.1/..., http://localhost:6379/... (Redis), or http://169.254.169.254/... (cloud metadata IMDS). Token + URL both flow; no DNS pinning → DNS rebinding also possible.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/mcp-config.ts:173-180 (scheme-only check); packages/adapters/src/mcp/http-transport.ts:44 `fetchFn(config.url, ...)`; packages/adapters/src/mcp/sse-transport.ts:69 same; Authorization header includes BUTLER_V5_MCP_TOKEN bearer (mcp-config.ts:146,200)
findings.fix_hint: At config-load time (mcp-config.ts:169): resolve hostname via dns.lookup, reject if address is in RFC1918 / 127.0.0.0/8 / 169.254.0.0/16 / ::1. Re-pin per request for DNS-rebinding mitigation. Add opt-in env var BUTLER_V5_MCP_ALLOW_PRIVATE for dev.

findings.title: D69-SEC-009 regression: subagent-worker logs LLM reply excerpt to stderr (PII/secret leak)
findings.description: Re-checked post-D69: logger.warn at subagent-worker.ts:581 still writes first 80 chars of every LLM reply: `logger.warn(`[subagent-worker] LLM replied: ${result.content.slice(0, 80)}`)`. LLM replies commonly echo user-supplied secrets, tokens, password fragments, or content the operator marked sensitive. Same PII-log class closed in D62 (audit #1 SF-04); D69 ship did not propagate the fix to subagent-worker.ts. Stderr is captured by launchd / systemd / docker logs.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/subagent-worker.ts:581 `logger.warn(`[subagent-worker] LLM replied: ${result.content.slice(0, 80)}`)`
findings.fix_hint: Replace with category-only log: `logger.warn(`[subagent-worker] LLM replied: 80 chars, role=${role}`)` — never slice content. Run reply through existing secret-redact.ts helper before logging if length-only is insufficient.

findings.title: D70 pre-scoped SEC-11: Slack url_verification challenge has no team_id allowlist or rate limit
findings.description: D70 pre-scoped SEC-11. url_verification handler returns the Slack challenge echo unconditionally (routes.ts:344) — by design (Slack onboarding handshake requires skipping signature verification per D63 T4 audit #9 F-01). Two attack surfaces remain open: (a) no team_id allowlist — any attacker can confirm endpoint is Slack-aware and probe it; (b) no rate limit — a malicious client can flood challenge POSTs to consume Hono event-loop and sliver through the wider Slack handler. Note: D69-SEC-011 (defer) is now promoted because rate-limit attack is trivial and team_id allowlist is a one-line config.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/routes.ts:333-346 — `if (parsed.kind !== 'challenge') { ... verify ... } if (parsed.kind === 'challenge') { return c.json({ challenge: parsed.challenge }) }`; Slack webhook payload includes team_id but the parser (slack-protocol.ts:54-60) does not surface it; no env-driven allowlist anywhere in apps/api
findings.fix_hint: Add BUTLER_V5_SLACK_TEAM_ID allowlist (comma-separated) check after parsing url_verification: reject when present and not in allowlist. Add a per-IP throttle (10/min) on the slack/events route. Surface team_id in parseSlackEventPayload return type.

findings.title: Channel outbound media path traversal via [[media:]] attachment path from LLM reply
findings.description: parseChannelOutboundMedia (channel-outbound-media.ts:40) extracts `[[media:PATH]]` from the LLM-generated reply and passes rawPath to isAllowedOutboundMediaPath (channel-outbound-media.ts:69). isAllowedOutboundMediaPath checks resolved.startsWith(`${root}/`) — but path normalization on `[[media:../../../../etc/passwd]]` produces a resolved path that DOES start with `./` which is in the implicit cwd root; only the allowlist root gates matter. However, BUTLER_V5_WORKSPACE / BUTLER_V5_TELEGRAM_MEDIA_DIR (channel-outbound-media.ts:60-67) are operator-controlled; a hostile reply that hits a path the operator mounted read-only (e.g. dotfile root) can still succeed where the operator didn't intend. Also: `basename(rawPath)` (line 51) does not strip path separators for the upstream Slack upload filename.
findings.evidence: channel-outbound-media.ts:73-76 `const resolved = resolve(isAbsolute(filePath) ? filePath : resolve(process.cwd(), filePath))`; line 75 `resolved === root || resolved.startsWith(`${root}/`)`; rawPath from LLM reply = untrusted
findings.fix_hint: Reject any rawPath containing `..`, `.`, or null bytes before resolve. Cross-check basename against an explicit ext allowlist. Log the resolved path + content-hash to operator audit.

findings.title: D69-SEC-021 regression: WS server has no per-conversationId subscriber cap (FD exhaustion)
findings.description: D69-SEC-021 (defer) confirmed still open. registerSubscriber (ws-routes.ts:114-131) adds ws to set without checking set.size — a single valid subscribe token + millions of parallel ws.connect attempts exhausts process FDs and OOMs Node. The token-mint endpoint has a 10K global cap (D63 T4 ws-subscribe.ts:9) but no per-conversation cap on actual subscribers. Bound: 100 MiB WS messages capped at D69 T4 (line 240) but socket count itself is uncapped.
findings.evidence: ws-routes.ts:114-131 `function registerSubscriber(conversationId, ws) { let set = subscribers.get(conversationId); if (!set) { set = new Set(); subscribers.set(conversationId, set) } set.add(ws) }`; no size guard
findings.fix_hint: Add `if (set.size >= MAX_SUBSCRIBERS_PER_CONVERSATION) { ws.close(1008, 'subscriber cap'); return }` before set.add. Suggested cap: 16 per conversationId.

findings.title: Channel inbound fromSubject/channelId/messageId lack length/format cap (resource amplification)
findings.description: D69-SEC-017 (defer) confirmed still open. handleChannelInbound (channel-inbound.ts:29) accepts any fromSubject/channelId/messageId with only `channelId.trim()` (line 42). A network-reachable attacker (post-auth, post-allowlist) can pass a 100 MB messageId; it flows into event-id `evt-${Date.now()}-channel-${input.messageId ?? 'no-msgid'}` (channel-inbound.ts:63) and conversationId; persisted into the event_store JSON column. Same pattern at routes.ts:170 `evt-${Date.now()}-wechat-${body.messageId}` — untrusted messageId from /v1/wechat/inbound.
findings.evidence: channel-inbound.ts:42 `channelId = input.channelId.trim()`; channel-inbound.ts:63 `evt-${Date.now()}-channel-${input.messageId ?? 'no-msgid'}`; routes.ts:170 `evt-${Date.now()}-wechat-${body.messageId ?? 'no-msgid'}`
findings.fix_hint: Cap each to 256 chars + charset [A-Za-z0-9_:.-]+ at route layer; reject others with 400. Apply same cap inside /v1/wechat/inbound before flow into the event bridge.

findings.title: D69-SEC-014 / D70 pre-scoped SEC-14: interpretQrStatus bot_token not Secret<T>-wrapped
findings.description: D70 pre-scoped SEC-14. Re-checked: QrStatusAction.confirmed.token (ilink.ts:220) is still a plain `string`. wechat-login.ts:63 reads `action = interpretQrStatus(status.value)` and wechat-login.ts:75 writes token to env file via upsertWechatEnvFile. Any consumer (or future console.error for debug) can accidentally `JSON.stringify(action)` and dump token to logs. The Secret<T> newtype was proposed in D69-SEC-014 fix_hint but never adopted.
findings.evidence: packages/adapters/src/wechat/ilink.ts:220 `token: String(response['bot_token'] ?? '')`; cli/src/wechat-login.ts:71-79 reads action.token and writes to .env
findings.fix_hint: Wrap token in Secret<string> newtype with a redact() method. Same pattern as packages/runtime/src/secret-redact.ts (if exists); if not, create packages/domain/src/secret.ts and adopt in ilink.ts.

findings.title: D69-SEC-023 regression: env-file.ts upserts secrets without chmod on existing files
findings.description: writeFileSync(path, ..., { mode: 0o600 }) (env-file.ts:43) only applies mode on creation. If the operator's pre-existing .env has mode 0o644 (typical when hand-edited or copied from a backup), the WECHAT_TOKEN line will be written into a world-readable file. Node.js writeFileSync with mode option does NOT chmod existing files. A multi-user Linux box (shared dev host, CI runner with non-default umask) is the realistic threat model.
findings.evidence: packages/adapters/src/wechat/env-file.ts:43 `writeFileSync(path, ..., { encoding: 'utf8', mode: 0o600 })`; behavior documented in Node.js fs docs
findings.fix_hint: After writeFileSync, call `if (existsSync(path)) chmodSync(path, 0o600)` regardless of file existence. Pattern: write, then chmod, then verify with statSync.

findings.title: D69-SEC-022 regression: default wechat dmPolicy is 'open' (default-permissive DM)
findings.description: dmPolicy defaults to 'open' (ilink-poller.ts:120). Operator who doesn't set WECHAT_DM_POLICY=allowlist accepts inbound from any wechat user, who can then drive LLM tool calls on the owner's behalf. ilink-poller.ts:141 `isDmAllowed(inbound.fromUserId, dmPolicy, allowedUserIds)` — open policy returns true unconditionally. ilink-config.ts (referenced in D69-SEC-022) was rechecked: same pattern.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/ilink-poller.ts:120 `const dmPolicy = deps.dmPolicy ?? 'open'`; ilink-poller.test.ts:97-105 documents the 'GIBBERISH coerces to open' default; the runtime default is identical
findings.fix_hint: Default to 'allowlist' and seed with BUTLER_OWNER_WECHAT_ID automatically (read from env). Require explicit opt-in to 'open' via BUTLER_V5_DM_POLICY_OPT_IN=1.

findings.title: Audit-event detail can echo raw LLM content via 'tool_call' subagent audit path
findings.description: Same code path as D70-SEC-004 but the regression is broader: subagent-worker.ts:581 also surfaces `result.content.slice(0,80)` into `logger.warn` which is captured by the audit-reader.ts -> replay path. A subsequent replay API owner call returns audit_event records whose `subject` field may include the sliced content (subject column = actor; see audit-reader.ts:21-22 'subject -> tool_name' mapping comment). On a 5xx path or replay failure, the raw token fragment becomes part of an audit row.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/subagent-worker.ts:581 `logger.warn(`[subagent-worker] LLM replied: ${result.content.slice(0, 80)}`)`; apps/api/src/lib/fatigue/audit-reader.ts:54-60 maps subject -> tool_name but doesn't redact
findings.fix_hint: Same as D70-SEC-004 — remove content slice from log. Additionally add subject-field redaction at audit-reader.ts:54 for any substring matching common secret patterns (token, password, xoxb-, xoxp-, etc.).

findings.title: Slack/Telegram outbound errors include raw upstream body slice in deliveryReason
findings.description: D69-SEC-012 (defer) confirmed still open. channel-outbound.ts surfaces `description` from Telegram error JSON or `parsed.error` from Slack into `deliveryReason`. The Slack raw slice path (slack-outbound.ts:63 `reason: 'slack API non-JSON: ' + raw.slice(0, 200)`) is the worst — on non-JSON upstream responses, 200 chars of raw upstream body is embedded in the operator-visible reply metadata. Telegram's `description` from api.telegram.org can include sensitive details (e.g. bot was kicked, chat not found).
findings.evidence: packages/adapters/src/slack/slack-outbound.ts:63 `reason: `slack API non-JSON: ${raw.slice(0, 200)}``; apps/api/src/channel-outbound.ts:131/147/198/211 surface deliveryReason; channels/inbound returns deliveryReason in JSON response (routes.ts:375, 432)
findings.fix_hint: Log raw upstream body to operator stderr at error level; return fixed generic reason ('upstream non-JSON response' or 'telegram API error') to caller. Same fix for Slack error field.

findings.title: D69-SEC-019 regression: audit-log JSONL parser has no per-line byte cap
findings.description: readRecentSubagentAudit (audit-log.ts:84-108) reads the entire file via readFileSync(path, 'utf8') and JSON.parse's each line. A malicious or corrupt log entry could be a multi-MB single line — parser would buffer fully into memory before parsing. With audit_log.txt on a slow disk this is also a CPU+IO spike.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/audit-log.ts:92 `const raw = readFileSync(path, 'utf8')`; lines 96-107 split + JSON.parse without length cap
findings.fix_hint: Cap per-line length to e.g. 64 KiB before JSON.parse; truncate or skip longer lines with operator stderr warning. Stream the file (line-by-line via readline) for O(1) memory.

findings.title: D69-SEC-027 regression: Math.random used for X-WECHAT-UIN header (predictable RNG)
findings.description: ilink-protocol.ts:166 generates X-WECHAT-UIN with `Math.floor(Math.random() * 1_000_000_000)`. Math.random is not cryptographically strong and is predictable to an attacker who can observe a few UIN values. The WeChat iLink server uses UIN for session correlation; predictability weakens upstream dedup and reduces entropy floor for any downstream consumer that keys off it. Same finding as D69-SEC-027 (defer) — not closed.
findings.evidence: packages/adapters/src/wechat/ilink-protocol.ts:166 `"X-WECHAT-UIN": String(Math.floor(Math.random() * 1_000_000_000))`
findings.fix_hint: Use `randomBytes(8).toString('hex')` or `randomInt(0, 1_000_000_000)`. If WeChat protocol requires a numeric UIN, accept the entropy reduction but seed from crypto.

findings.title: D69-SEC-024 regression: WS server logs conversationId verbatim on every error
findings.description: All 4 WS error handlers log raw conversationId to stderr: `console.error(`[ws-routes] failed to serialize event for ${conversationId}:`, err)` at lines 91, 102, 217, 245. conversationId format `c-${projectId}-${ts}` (routes.ts:66) embeds projectId + timestamp; it is a PII identifier cross-referenced with content. Same finding as D69-SEC-024 (defer) — not closed.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/ws-routes.ts:91, 102, 217, 245 — all use `${conversationId}` in console.error
findings.fix_hint: Redact or hash conversationId in WS error logs: keep only last 4 chars + a SHA-256 prefix. Centralize via a redactConversationId() helper.

findings.title: WS server extracts token + conversationId from req.url without decode validation
findings.description: extractQueryParam (ws-routes.ts:134-151) splits req.url on '?' and '&' then decodeURIComponent. No length cap, no character set restriction. A token or conversationId of 100 MB will be allocated into a string. Same for resolveWsIdentity (line 198) which compares the parsed conversationId against rec.conversationId — both attacker-controlled bytes. Token validation (lookupSubscribeToken) is O(1) but the decode step is unbounded.
findings.evidence: ws-routes.ts:134-151 `function extractQueryParam(url, name)` — no length cap; ws-routes.ts:198-215 `function resolveWsIdentity` — no length cap on token or conversationId
findings.fix_hint: Cap raw URL length at the upgrade handler (e.g. reject if req.url.length > 1024). Cap extracted param length at 512 chars; reject longer with close(1008).

findings.title: Telegram sendMessage error path lacks timeout enforcement (calls hang forever)
findings.description: sendTelegramOutboundMessage uses AbortController with 15s timeout (channel-outbound.ts:41). However on the non-JSON success path (line 73-74), `await fetchFn(url, ...)` with `signal: controller.signal` is correct — but the JSON.parse path (line 56-60) catches parse errors and returns; if fetchFn returns a Response whose body buffers large content beyond the 15s timeout, the controller.abort() fires but only after the fetch resolved. There is no max-bytes cap on the response body before parsing.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/channel-outbound.ts:45-50 fetchFn with timeoutMs; line 51 `const raw = await res.text()` — no byte cap
findings.fix_hint: Cap response body to e.g. 64 KiB via stream + reader.cancel() if exceeded; surface 'telegram response too large' in reason.

findings.title: wechat-login logs accountId to stdout (PII correlation)
findings.description: wechat-login.ts:80 `log(`微信连接成功，account_id=${action.accountId}`)` writes the iLink bot account ID (a stable user identifier) to stdout. CI logs / docker logs are typically retained; accountId + baseUrl combo lets an observer correlate butler deployments. Lower severity than token leak but same class.
findings.evidence: cli/src/wechat-login.ts:80 `log(`微信连接成功，account_id=${action.accountId}`)`
findings.fix_hint: Hash or redact accountId before log; print only first 4 chars. Same for log(`已写入 ${opts.envPath}`) — env path is fine but normalize.

findings.title: D69-SEC-016 / D70 pre-scoped SEC-16: No HTTP security headers on API responses
findings.description: D70 pre-scoped SEC-16. Re-checked: no Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, or X-Frame-Options set anywhere in apps/api/src/. The Hono app is constructed at index.ts:37 with `app = new Hono()` and the only middleware is body-limit (index.ts:38-53). Slack/Telegram webhook handlers (routes.ts:316, 394) return text/json bodies and are internet-facing when configured — defense-in-depth headers (HSTS + nosniff + Referrer-Policy) protect against MIME confusion + downgrade + referrer leaks. Same finding as D69-SEC-016 (defer) — not closed.
findings.evidence: grep -rn 'Strict-Transport\|X-Content-Type\|X-Frame\|Content-Security-Policy\|Referrer-Policy' apps/api/src returns 0 hits; apps/api/src/index.ts:37-53 shows only the body-limit middleware
findings.fix_hint: Add `app.use('*', setSecurityHeaders)` middleware setting: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, X-Frame-Options: DENY. Mirror common/security.md CSP guidance for any owner-facing HTML.

findings.title: D69-SEC-015 regression: Inbound shared-secret compare uses non-constant-time !== (timing side-channel)
findings.description: D69-SEC-015 (defer) confirmed still open. routes.ts:89 `if (headerInboundSecret.trim() !== expectedInboundSecret)` — plain string equality leaks byte-by-byte comparison timing. Slack verifySlackSignature uses crypto.timingSafeEqual (slack-protocol.ts:30-32). An attacker who can issue many auth probes can recover the secret via statistical timing analysis. Same risk on routes.ts:279 (channel-inbound secret) and channel-inbound.ts:165 (telegram webhook secret).
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/routes.ts:89, 279 plain !== / ===; apps/api/src/channel-inbound.ts:165 plain ===; packages/adapters/src/slack/slack-protocol.ts:30-32 uses timingSafeEqual — inconsistent
findings.fix_hint: Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(a), Buffer.from(b))` after length-normalize. Mirror slack-protocol.ts:30-32 pattern. Pad to equal length first since timingSafeEqual requires it.

findings.title: Telegram webhook secret compare uses non-constant-time === (timing side-channel)
findings.description: telegramWebhookAuthorized (channel-inbound.ts:155-166) compares secrets with `(headerSecret ?? '').trim() === expected`. Same timing-leak class as D70-SEC-021. telegramWebhookAuthorized is called on every inbound webhook POST (routes.ts:399). Telegram attackers can mount online timing attacks over a noisy internet link with sufficient probes.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/channel-inbound.ts:165 `(headerSecret ?? '').trim() === expected`; called from routes.ts:399
findings.fix_hint: Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(...), Buffer.from(...))` after equal-length pad. Cover all 3 secret compare sites: routes.ts:89/279 and channel-inbound.ts:165.

findings.title: Channel inbound shared secret compare uses non-constant-time === (timing side-channel)
findings.description: /v1/channel/inbound (routes.ts:260-315) compares BUTLER_V5_CHANNEL_INBOUND_SECRET against x-channel-inbound-secret header with `headerChannelSecret.trim() !== expectedChannelSecret` (routes.ts:279). Same timing-leak class. Generic channel intake is a smaller attack surface (allowlist-gated) but still warrants constant-time.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/routes.ts:279 `if (headerChannelSecret.trim() !== expectedChannelSecret)`
findings.fix_hint: Same as D70-SEC-021 — use timingSafeEqual with padded equal-length.

findings.title: Hono body-limit middleware accepts Content-Length: 0 as valid (low-impact bypass vector)
findings.description: index.ts:42-51: `if (contentLengthHeader === null) return 411 chunked reject; if (Number.isFinite(declared) && declared > MAX_BODY_BYTES) return 413`. Edge cases: Content-Length: 0 is accepted (a POST /v1/wechat/inbound with body length 0 passes middleware then is rejected by the route's body parse — fine). However Content-Length with leading whitespace ('  100') or non-ASCII characters is not validated: Number('  100') === 100 but Number('\u3000 100') === NaN — falls through to allow. Theoretical only — no exploit path found; route-layer body parse downstream still rejects malformed bodies.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/index.ts:42-50 — uses `Number(contentLengthHeader)` without strict-validate; no .trim()
findings.fix_hint: Use `parseInt(contentLengthHeader.trim(), 10)` with strict-digit check `if (!/^\d+$/.test(contentLengthHeader.trim())) return 400`. Mirror existing patterns elsewhere in the codebase.

findings.title: WS subscribe endpoint: conversationId not bound to authenticated caller
findings.description: D69 T4 SEC-3 closed auth (routes.ts:451-462 now requires x-inbound-secret) but the bind logic remains broken: any caller with the shared secret can mint a token for ANY conversationId. The token is then usable to subscribe to that conversation's event push channel. There is no caller-side ownership check. IDOR class: caller A subscribes to caller B's real-time events. Shared-secret callers (e.g. owner CLI + per-tenant inbound bridge) cannot be distinguished at this seam.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/routes.ts:480 `const issued = issueSubscribeToken(parsedId.value)` — no caller-binding; parsedId.value is from caller-supplied body; lookupSubscribeToken (ws-subscribe.ts:48) returns the conversationId without re-checking caller
findings.fix_hint: Bind conversationId to authenticated caller: include caller-id (or per-tenant secret-derivative) in token generation; on lookup, verify the token's bound caller matches the upgrader's authenticated subject.

findings.title: WS subscriber registry holds unbounded conversationId entries (Map memory growth)
findings.description: subscribers (ws-routes.ts:45) is a module-level `Map<string, Set<WebSocket>>` that grows per conversationId. Empty sets ARE removed on teardown (line 128-130) — good — but the map itself never has a hard cap on conversationId count. An attacker who mints 10K subscribe tokens (D63 T4 cap) targeting distinct conversationIds, then opens a WS for each, then drops — the map correctly cleans up. BUT: a misconfigured caller that doesn't drop (WS keepalive from the caller's POV) leaves the entry alive indefinitely, with TTL = none. After process restart the map resets. Indefinite retention until restart = long-lived resource leak.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/ws-routes.ts:45 `export const subscribers: Map<string, Set<WsWebSocket>> = new Map()`; no expiry / no max-key cap
findings.fix_hint: Add per-conversationId idle TTL (e.g. 1h after last subscriber disconnect, drop the key). Bound total key count: refuse new keys above N=10K with ws.close(1013, 'try again later').

findings.title: Slack url_verification bypass: any client can probe endpoint liveness
findings.description: routes.ts:344 returns `c.json({ challenge: parsed.challenge })` unconditionally for url_verification. Without team_id allowlist (D70-SEC-005) or rate limit, this is an info-disclosure vector: an attacker can probe to confirm endpoint is Slack-aware, deduce BUTLER_V5_SLACK_ENABLED state, and use the endpoint as a single-shot timing oracle (challenge echo + response time).
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/routes.ts:344 `if (parsed.kind === 'challenge') { return c.json({ challenge: parsed.challenge }) }`
findings.fix_hint: Fold into D70-SEC-005 fix: add team_id allowlist + per-IP throttle. As minimum, rate-limit the challenge branch.

findings.title: Channel outbound fetchFn has no max response size (MIME confusion / decompression bomb)
findings.description: All channel outbound fetch calls (slack, telegram, channel-outbound-media) use `await res.text()` or `await res.json()` without capping bytes. A malicious upstream API returning a 1 GB response body will be fully buffered. For text bodies the timingSafeEqual concern doesn't apply, but a Telegram 200 with 100 MB gzip body would be inflated into 1 GB+ before JSON.parse. Decompression bombs are an emerging DoS class.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/channel-outbound.ts:51 `const raw = await res.text()` — no size cap; slack-outbound.ts:58 `const raw = await res.text()`; channel-outbound-media.ts:124-125 same
findings.fix_hint: Wrap `res.text()` in a byte-capped reader (Node 18+ ReadableStream `getReader({ mode: 'byob' })`). Cap at e.g. 1 MiB for non-media endpoints, 50 MiB for media endpoints.

findings.title: Telegram webhook route has no chat_id allowlist (post-auth spam amplification)
findings.description: parseTelegramUpdate (channel-inbound.ts:119-153) accepts any user_id as `fromSubject` and flows into handleChannelInbound → runButlerLoop with no chat_id or user_id allowlist. The generic channel intake (/v1/channel/inbound) has BUTLER_V5_CHANNEL_ALLOWLIST (channel-config.ts:18-22), but the telegram webhook (routes.ts:394) has no equivalent. Once a telegram bot_token is configured, any telegram user can DM the bot and drive LLM tool calls.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/channel-inbound.ts:145 `fromSubject: String(userId)`; apps/api/src/routes.ts:394-450 telegram webhook handler; no BUTLER_V5_TELEGRAM_USER_ALLOWLIST env anywhere
findings.fix_hint: Add BUTLER_V5_TELEGRAM_USER_ALLOWLIST (comma-separated chat_id / user_id) gate inside channel-inbound.ts:75 before runButlerLoop. Default-deny (empty allowlist = reject all).

findings.title: Slack events route has no user_id allowlist (post-auth spam amplification)
findings.description: parseSlackEventPayload (slack-protocol.ts:81-104) accepts any user ID and flows into handleChannelInbound with no allowlist. Same class as D70-SEC-029. After signature verification (post-D63 T4 F-01), any Slack user in the bot's workspace can DM the bot and trigger LLM-driven tool calls.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/routes.ts:354-360 handleChannelInbound call; no BUTLER_V5_SLACK_USER_ALLOWLIST; slack-protocol.ts:86 `if (typeof user !== 'string' || ...) return ignore` — string check only, no allowlist
findings.fix_hint: Add BUTLER_V5_SLACK_USER_ALLOWLIST (comma-separated Slack user IDs) gate in routes.ts:354 before handleChannelInbound. Default-deny.

findings.title: MCP stdio transport spawns command without path allowlist
findings.description: parseMcpConnectionConfig stdio branch (mcp-config.ts:148-166) accepts BUTLER_V5_MCP_COMMAND as an executable path with no allowlist. An operator who follows a malicious manifest example or an attacker who can write to the manifest file can spawn arbitrary binaries. resolveManifestStdioArgs (mcp-config.ts:156) further resolves relative args from manifest path — relative-path command injection vector.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/mcp-config.ts:148-152 stdio branch returns command + args directly; mcp-config.ts:156 `args = resolveManifestStdioArgs(manifestPath, args)`; no path validation
findings.fix_hint: Validate command against an explicit BUTLER_V5_MCP_COMMAND_ALLOWLIST (absolute paths). Reject any command outside the allowlist. Reject args with `..` or shell metacharacters.

findings.title: WS origin allowlist treats 0.0.0.0 bind as loopback (logic ambiguity)
findings.description: isOriginAllowedForWsUpgrade (ws-routes.ts:171-196) treats `boundHost === '0.0.0.0'` as a loopback bind (line 176) and applies the loopback-origin-or-env-allowlist rule. However 0.0.0.0 explicitly means 'all interfaces' — NOT loopback. An operator who sets WS_HOST=0.0.0.0 expecting a loopback-only WS server would have it bound to all interfaces, exposing the WS endpoint publicly, but the loopback-origin branch still allows loopback origins without checking the env allowlist. Origin allowlist is therefore bypassable via loopback Origin header on a non-loopback bind.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/ws-routes.ts:171-196 — `if (boundHost === '127.0.0.1' || ... || boundHost === '0.0.0.0')`; line 177 `if (isLoopbackBind)` triggers loopback-origin branch even for 0.0.0.0
findings.fix_hint: Treat 0.0.0.0 as 'public bind' and ALWAYS require BUTLER_V5_WS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS env var. Remove 0.0.0.0 from isLoopbackBind set. Document: loopback binds = 127.0.0.1 / ::1 / localhost only.

findings.title: Telegram outbound reply text is not length-capped before sending
findings.description: clipOutboundText (channel-outbound.ts:23-27) clips to 3900 chars for both Telegram and Slack outbound. Good. But /v1/wechat/inbound (routes.ts:245-258) returns the raw `loopResult.reply` to the inbound caller without re-clipping — an LLM reply that drifts to 10K chars is returned to the wechat client. Not a server-side security boundary, but a DoS vector for the caller / log file.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/routes.ts:248-249 `reply: reply` — no clip; loopResult.reply can be unbounded
findings.fix_hint: Apply a global `clipReply(loopResult.reply, 30000)` at routes.ts:249 before returning to caller. Truncate at last newline for clean breaks.
